{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-wi-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"55bd44fb1e32064365fd18c53fa7c4dfe206b679e6de55b8298ea2dbdd2c2477","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-wi-class-d:lineage:41","source_registry_sha256":"9dcfc0d0c3044debd01d4cb03103f48fb860797364a23b2cb56d36c868619a64","source_liveness_sha256":"4ca51030ff51b3372629ada1c05ad91f501dabccdcf7931dab678c717e7bb9b6"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Dangerous driving behaviors: alcohol and drugs, implied consent, distracted driving and drowsy driving","heading":"C — Dangerous driving behaviors: how alcohol and drugs impair driving, the underage zero alcohol rule, controlled substances, medication labels, implied consent and the PAC test, cell phone and distraction rules, and the warning signs of drowsy driving","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Dangerous driving behaviors: how alcohol and drugs impair driving, the underage zero alcohol rule, controlled substances, medication labels, implied consent and the PAC test, cell phone and distraction rules, and the warning signs of drowsy driving
Knowledge domain: the behaviors that most raise crash risk — impaired, distracted and drowsy driving — and the Wisconsin rules that apply to them, including the zero alcohol limit for underage drivers and the implied consent law.

FACT_ID: sec10-F01 | anchor: A01
Alcohol, drugs and other substances change how you think and decide, making it hard to judge the distance, speed and movement of other vehicles. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F02 | anchor: A01
Driving under the influence of any drug is illegal, and that includes both prescription and over-the-counter drugs. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F03 | anchor: A01
Drunk or drugged drivers have a higher chance of being in a crash. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F04 | anchor: A01
For drivers under the age of 21 the legal alcohol concentration is 0.00%, so they may not have any alcohol in their system while driving. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F05 | anchor: A01
Having any amount of a controlled substance in your system counts the same as driving impaired. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F06 | anchor: A01
Studies cited by the handbook show that marijuana users make more mistakes while driving. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F07 | anchor: A01
Before driving after taking a prescription or over-the-counter medicine, read the warning label for side effects. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F08 | anchor: A01
A medicine label that warns against operating heavy machinery applies to driving a motor vehicle too. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F09 | anchor: A01
If you have been drinking, get a ride home from a sober friend or relative, or ask a bartender to call a cab. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F10 | anchor: A01
Only time sobers a person up. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F11 | anchor: A01
Under the implied consent law, when an officer requests a prohibited alcohol concentration (PAC) test, you are required to agree to it. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F12 | anchor: A01
A PAC test uses a breathalyzer or a blood test to find out whether you have a measurable amount of alcohol. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F13 | anchor: A01
If you refuse a PAC test, the officer must arrest you for violating the Implied Consent Law. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F14 | anchor: A01
Refusing a PAC test costs you your driving privileges for at least one year, along with other consequences. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F15 | anchor: A01
Distraction is dangerous, so concentrate on the driving task and keep your eyes on the road. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F16 | anchor: A01
Do not drive wearing headsets or headphones that cover or sit in both ears. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F17 | anchor: A01
Keep the radio volume low enough that you can hear emergency vehicles. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F18 | anchor: A01
Avoid answering your phone while driving; if you need it, pull over safely first. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F19 | anchor: A01
Instruction permit and probationary license holders may use a cell phone while driving only to report an emergency. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F20 | anchor: A01
Regular license holders should still avoid cell phones while driving and use the vehicle's hands-free option if a call is necessary. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F21 | anchor: A02
Pull over to a safe place if you need to read directions, and eat only when the car is parked. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec10-F22 | anchor: A02
Keep pets in a carrier or have a passenger hold them. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec10-F23 | anchor: A02
Do not hang objects from the rearview mirror or cover your windows with decals. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec10-F24 | anchor: A02
Drowsy driving means driving while very tired from too little sleep, which can also come from an untreated sleep disorder or a long work shift. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec10-F25 | anchor: A02
Get a good night's sleep before driving, since teen and young adult drivers face a higher risk of drowsiness-related crashes. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec10-F26 | anchor: A02
Pull over and rest if you keep yawning or blinking, drift out of your lane, or hit the rumble strip at the road's edge. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

Misconceptions: nothing but time sobers you up, so waiting is the only fix; a legal prescription or over-the-counter medicine can still make driving illegal if it impairs you; a heavy machinery warning on a label includes your car; refusing a breath or blood test does not avoid trouble, it brings arrest and a loss of driving privileges; drivers under twenty-one get no alcohol allowance at all; a regular license does not make phone use safe, it only changes the rule from banned to avoid.
Mnemonics: under twenty-one means zero point zero zero; refuse the test, lose the license; permit and probationary drivers phone only for emergencies; yawn, drift or rumble means pull over and rest.
Glossary: PAC means prohibited alcohol concentration; implied consent means the Wisconsin law requiring you to take a PAC test when an officer asks, with penalties for refusing; controlled substance means a drug regulated by law; breathalyzer means a breath test device that measures alcohol; hands-free means using a phone without holding it; rumble strip means grooves at the road edge that vibrate when driven over.
